The most important and widely used meaning of pluck as a noun is courage — but not just any kind of courage. It is a very specific, warm, and admirable kind of courage: the guts to keep going, keep trying, or stand firm even when things are hard, scary, or stacked against you.

Think of it this way: if a small, underdog boxer gets knocked down in a fight but refuses to stay down — getting back up again and again despite being outmatched — people would say "That kid has real pluck." It is the courage of the determined heart, not the courage of the powerful person who has nothing to fear.

This is important. Several words mean courage — bravery, boldness, nerve, guts, courage itself — but pluck has its own flavour:

  • It suggests courage despite difficulty or disadvantage. A mighty warrior who easily defeats an enemy shows strength. But a young, inexperienced person who faces that same enemy without backing down? That person shows pluck.
  • It has a spirited, lively quality to it. It is active, determined courage — not just the absence of fear, but the will to push through regardless of fear.
  • It carries a tone of warmth and admiration. When someone calls you plucky, they are rooting for you. It is the word people use for underdogs they love and respect.
  • It is slightly informal and old-fashioned in feel, which gives it a charming quality. You will find it often in literature, sports commentary, and storytelling.

Here are clear examples so you can see exactly how it is used:

"Nobody expected the small team to win the championship, but their pluck carried them through every match."

"It took enormous pluck for her to stand up in front of the board and challenge their decision alone."

"The villagers showed great pluck in rebuilding their homes after the flood, even when they had almost nothing left."

"I admire his pluck — most people would have given up months ago."

In every example, notice the same thing: the person is in a tough spot, but they face it with a fighting spirit. That fighting spirit is their pluck.

You will often see "pluck" used with these words:

  • Show pluck — to demonstrate this kind of courage
  • Have pluck — to possess it as a quality
  • Real pluck / great pluck — used to emphasise the degree
  • A lot of pluck / some pluck — to describe the amount
  • Admire someone's pluck — to respect this quality in them

These words are close in meaning to pluck (as a noun):

  • Guts — very informal, means the same determined, inner courage
  • Nerve — the coolness and boldness to do something hard
  • Backbone — suggests moral firmness and refusal to be pushed around
  • Mettle — the quality of someone's character when tested
  • Spirit — the lively energy and determination within someone
  • Fortitude — more formal; the strength to endure hardship

Among all of these, pluck is unique because it most strongly suggests the underdog spirit — someone smaller, weaker, or less powerful who refuses to back down.

• Cowardice — the failure of courage
  • Timidity — being too fearful and hesitant
  • Spinelessness — lacking the backbone to stand firm

"Pluck" as a noun has two other, rarer meanings you should know so you are never caught off guard:

1. A quick pull or tug.
When you physically pull at something with your fingers — a string, a sleeve, a feather — that single pulling action can be called a pluck.

"She gave a pluck at his sleeve to get his attention."
"With a gentle pluck of the guitar string, the music began."

This meaning is closely related to the verb to pluck (meaning to pull something). As a standalone noun, it is not very common in everyday speech, but you may encounter it.

2. The internal organs of a slaughtered animal.
In the context of butchery and cooking, pluck refers to the heart, liver, and lungs of an animal taken together. This is a very old, specialised use. If you ever come across a traditional recipe or old text mentioning "sheep's pluck" or "ox pluck," this is what it means. You are unlikely to encounter this meaning in everyday conversation, but it is worth knowing.

To put it plainly:

  • Meaning 1 (main): Pluck = determined, spirited courage, especially of someone facing the odds. This is what the word almost always means today.
  • Meaning 2 (rare): A quick pull or tug at something.
  • Meaning 3 (very rare/specialised): The edible organs of an animal.

When you hear or read pluck as a noun, it will almost certainly be referring to that admirable, gutsy, underdog courage. Remember the image of someone small and disadvantaged who refuses to give up — that is pluck.
